title: Objects
summary: An object groups related values under names. One object could store a book's title, author and page count.
introduction: An object groups related values under names. One object could store a book's title, author and page count. Make a small book record. Read a named value, change it and add a new fact without mixing up the labels.
learningObjectives: Create an object literal and read properties with dot and bracket notation
Add, change and delete properties and handle missing ones safely
Write methods that use this to access the object's own data
Loop over keys, values and entries and copy an object without sharing it

blocks.text: An **object literal** is a list of `key: value` pairs in braces. Keys are strings (quotes are optional when the key is a valid identifier) and values can be anything, including other objects, arrays and functions. Read a property with a dot when you know its name while writing the code, and with square brackets when the name is stored in a variable or contains characters such as spaces or hyphens.

blocks.title: book.key is not book[key]
blocks.text: `book.key` looks for a property literally called `key`; it does not read the variable. When the property name is in a variable, you must use brackets: `book[key]`. This is the most common mistake with objects and it fails silently, returning `undefined`.

Properties can hold objects and arrays, so you chain accesses: `order.customer.address.city`. Reading a property that does not exist gives `undefined`, but reading a property *of* `undefined` throws a `TypeError`. **Optional chaining** `?.` stops the chain and returns `undefined` as soon as it meets `null` or `undefined`, and the nullish coalescing operator `??` supplies a fallback. The `in` operator checks whether a key exists at all.

blocks.text: A function stored in a property is a **method**. Inside a method, `this` refers to the object the method was called on, which is how one method can work for any object that has the same shape. The shorthand `deposit(amount) {...}` is the modern way to write a method inside a literal.

`this` is decided by *how* a function is called, not where it is written: `account.describe()` sets it to `account`. Arrow functions do not have their own `this`, so do not use them for methods in a literal; the [Modern Syntax](/tutorials/javascript/es6-features) lesson explains when that behaviour is useful instead.

`Object.keys`, `Object.values` and `Object.entries` turn an object into arrays, which means every array method from the previous lesson becomes available. `Object.entries` gives `[key, value]` pairs that you can unpack directly in a `for...of` loop.

Assigning an object to another variable creates an **alias**, not a copy: both names point at the same object. To get an independent copy, spread the object into a new literal (`{ ...original }`). That copy is **shallow**, meaning nested objects are still shared; `structuredClone(original)` makes a deep copy. Comparing with `===` asks 'is this the same object?', never 'do these have the same contents?'.
`JSON.stringify` converts an object into text, which is useful for printing it on one line or comparing contents. The [Fetch and JSON](/tutorials/javascript/fetch-json) lesson covers it in depth.
When a function needs several settings, accept one object instead of a long list of parameters. Callers then name each value, can pass them in any order and can leave out the ones with defaults.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Add a `withdraw(amount)` method to the account object that refuses to go below zero and returns a message either way. Then write a loop over `Object.entries` that prints every property of `book` as `key = value`.

questions.question: The variable `field` holds the string `"email"`. Which expression reads the email property of `user`?
questions.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates the expression inside the brackets, so user[field] reads user.email. user.field would look for a property literally named field.

questions.question: `{ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }` evaluates to true because both objects have the same contents.
questions.explanation: === compares references. Two separate object literals are two different objects, so the result is false even though they look the same.
